title: Chemical Tank Called 'Unfit for Service' Before Deadly Failure, Investigators Find
summary:
A federal report released Friday reveals that a chemical tank at a Washington state paper mill was deemed "not fit for continued service" 10 months before it failed in May, killing 11 people in one of the deadliest U.S. workplace disasters in recent decades.

The U.S. Chemical Safety Board's update on the May 26 failure in Longview found that an inspection contractor had provided Nippon Dynawave Packaging Company with recommendations for internal inspections and shell repairs, but the company did none between a July 2025 inspection and the failure.

The tank released roughly 900,000 gallons of a caustic liquid known as white liquor, which is used to break down wood for paper products and can cause severe burns. The force blew out building walls. In addition to the deaths, several others and a firefighter were injured.

The July 2025 inspection found "significant thinning" below the minimum safe thickness in the lower regions of the tank. The contractor flagged it as "Priority 1: Not fit for continued service unless corrected," with a "high likelihood/consequence of failure." The report noted that the company did not remove the tank from operation or derate it for reduced service.

Board Chairperson Steve Owens said, "We are greatly concerned that the tank was not promptly removed from service or properly repaired after the clear findings in the inspection report."

The Association of Western Pulp and Paper Workers called the findings "deeply troubling," and a lawyer for the family of two brothers killed, Tyler and Bradley Covington, said they are "nothing short of alarming." Lawyer Kyle Findley stated, "When safety inspections and recommendations don't lead to action, danger becomes a reality that causes devastation to human life."

Senator Patty Murray said the community deserves answers and "every worker has the right to come home safely at the end of the day."

Nippon spokesperson Sam Jefferies said the company is cooperating fully and focusing on supporting affected families and reopening the facility. The investigation is ongoing.
why_it_matters: This disaster is a case study in why safety regulations only work when companies act on them; ignoring a written warning can cost lives. It also points to broader gaps in oversight that affect every industry where dangerous chemicals are stored and used.

background_read: The U.S. Chemical Safety Board (an independent federal agency that investigates industrial chemical accidents and issues safety recommendations) released the report described in this article.

The paper mill in Longview, Washington, is operated by Nippon Dynawave Packaging Company, the company named in the federal report; white liquor is a highly caustic chemical used in papermaking to break down wood fibers.

Industrial tanks are supposed to be inspected regularly, and when inspectors find dangerous thinning, the standard response is to take the tank out of service, repair it, or reduce how much it can safely hold.

The board's finding that the tank was marked 'not fit for continued service' but remained in operation fits a pattern seen in other workplace disasters: warnings are documented, but the gap between recommendation and action can have deadly consequences.

The Chemical Safety Board does not issue fines or criminal charges itself; its job is to establish what happened so other agencies, companies, and lawmakers can act, and to make recommendations that prevent the next accident.

perspectives.description: The company says it is cooperating fully with investigators and is focused on supporting affected families. Reopening the facility could preserve jobs in the community, if it can be done safely.

The report paints a damning picture: a tank labeled 'not fit for continued service' stayed in operation and later killed 11 people. The union, workers' families, and Senator Murray all point to the deadly gap between safety findings and real action.

This case fits a well-known pattern in industrial accidents: inspections document a problem, but the cost and disruption of fixing it cause delays until disaster forces action. The Chemical Safety Board can investigate and recommend, but it cannot enforce its proposals, so follow-through depends on companies and regulators.

The ongoing investigation could lead to stronger enforcement of inspection recommendations and legal consequences for the company. The key question is whether this tragedy will actually change how the industry treats 'not fit for continued service' warnings.
